42770536.title: Patterns of Children's Weight Change During Family-Based Weight Management Intervention and Associations With Outcome Through Follow-Up.
42770536.abstract: Introduction Understanding within-treatment weight change patterns may inform strategies to improve long-term outcomes for children with overweight/obesity. Methods Latent class modelling was applied to weekly weight change among 294 7-11-year-old children with overweight/obesity in behavioural weight management trials. Class differences in BMI z-score change through 1 year after treatment were examined using strict class assignment among completers (ANCOVA) or accounting for uncertainty in class assignment and missingness (Bolck, Croon and Hagenaars or BCH method). Results Three classes emerged-larger loss to stable weight (6% of children), consistent modest weight loss (43%) and moderate to decreasing weight loss (51%). During follow-up, the consistent modest weight loss class showed minimal change in BMI z-score whereas the other two classes increased (difference with moderate to decreasing weight loss class in ANCOVA = -0.096, p = 0.05; difference with large loss to stable class in BCH = -0.144, p = 0.017). The consistent modest weight loss class had the most favourable change from baseline through follow-up, better than the larger loss to stable weight class (ANCOVA difference = -0.189, p = 0.080; BCH difference = -0.186, p = 0.015). Conclusion Three patterns of within-treatment child weight change emerged, with modest consistent weight loss associated with more favourable distal child outcomes.

42698352.title: Comprehensive Treatment and Monthly 2 Year Follow-Up in Children With ADHD: Randomized Controlled Prospective Study.
42698352.abstract: ObjectivesTo evaluate the efficacy of regular monthly follow up in maintaining treatment gains versus follow up as needed in the community for children ages 6 to 12 years with ADHD.MethodsOne hundred and eighty six children, age 6 to 13 with DSM-IV diagnosed Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) (combined presentation) received 3 months of comprehensive treatment which included long-acting stimulant medication titrated to optimal dose (via parent and teacher reports) and weekly parent training groups and child social skills and academic training. After the 3 months of treatment, children were randomized to either monthly follow up by the research team (treatment group) or follow up as usual in the community (control group). Comprehensive evaluations occurred at 3 months at the end of the comprehensive treatment, and at 6, 12, 18, and 24 month follow-up.ResultsChildren in both groups improved significantly in all domains after the 3 months of intensive comprehensive treatment. Treatment gains were maintained during the 2 year follow up period in both groups. However, the Hyperactive/Impulsive rating in Conners scale by parent report and some teacher reports were worse in the community group during the follow-up period.ConclusionThe importance of the initial intensive comprehensive 3 month treatment cannot be underestimated as these treatments resulted in significant improvements which were maintained for 2 years in both groups. Factors such as social economic status and available community treatment which may have influenced these results are discussed.

42725565.title: Oral amoxicillin for management of fast breathing or chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs in children aged 2-59 months: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42725565.abstract: Background World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines recommend oral amoxicillin as first-line therapy for pneumonia in children aged 2-59 months. However, uncertainty remains regarding its effectiveness compared with no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia and with injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs. Methods We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (January 2000-August 2024) for randomised and quasi-randomised trials without language restrictions. Eligible studies compared oral amoxicillin vs. no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia or outpatient oral amoxicillin vs. inpatient injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs in children (2-59 months). Pooled relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using a random-effects model; certainty was assessed using GRADE. Results Four trials (n = 7,699) compared oral amoxicillin with no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia, and three (n = 4,864) compared oral with injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia. For fast breathing pneumonia, oral amoxicillin reduced treatment failure by 16% at day 14 (RR = 0.84; 95% CI = 0.75, 0.94, I 2 = 0%; moderate certainty). For chest indrawing pneumonia, treatment failure was similar between groups at day 6 (RR = 0.96; 95% CI = 0.83, 1.11) and day 14 (RR = 0.94; 95% CI = 0.79, 1.13), while mortality was 72% lower with oral amoxicillin (RR = 0.28; 95% CI = 0.09, 0.86). Serious adverse events did not differ between groups. Conclusions In children (2-59 months), oral amoxicillin significantly reduces treatment failure compared to no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia and is comparable to injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs. Notably, oral amoxicillin was associated with a 72% reduction in mortality compared with injectable antibiotics in children with chest-indrawing pneumonia, although absolute risk differences were small. These findings support its broader implementation as an accessible, programmatically feasible, and WHO-recommended option for pneumonia management in low-resource settings. Registration PROSPERO: CRD42023439851.

body.methods: We conducted a comprehensive search in the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Cochrane Register of Studies Online, PubMed®, and EMBASE® databases to identify relevant articles on randomised controlled trials or quasi-randomised trials published before 31 August 2024.
body.results: For the first research question (oral amoxicillin compared to no antibiotic treatment in children with fast breathing pneumonia), our initial database search on 31 August 2024 identified 6,645 records (Figure S1 in the Online Supplementary Document ). After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, 62 articles were selected for full-text review. Four relevant randomised controlled trials from three countries were included in our meta-analysis ( Table 1 ) that enrolled a total of 7,699 children aged 2–59 months with fast breathing pneumonia [ 15 , 27 – 29 ]. Of the included trials, three had a low risk of bias [ 15 , 27 , 28 ], and one trial had a high risk of bias [ 29 ] (Figure S2 in the Online Supplementary Document ). Three trials were conducted in low- or lower-middle-income countries [ 15 , 27 , 28 ] and one was conducted in low-income countries [ 29 ].
body.conclusion: These findings highlight the value of oral amoxicillin for wider implementation in LMICs, where healthcare resources are constrained as an accessible and programmatically feasible treatment option. Future research should aim to refine diagnostic criteria to guide antibiotic use more precisely, thereby improving pneumonia management while minimising the risk of antimicrobial resistance.

42910180.title: Giant Duodenal Perforation Secondary to Malaria in a 5-Year-Old Girl: Case Report and Review.
42910180.abstract: Background Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is rare in children, with complications like perforation being especially uncommon. Malaria, a major health burden in endemic regions, is associated with severe complications, but giant duodenal perforation as a direct consequence is remarkably rare. This report presents a 5-year-old girl with a giant duodenal perforation secondary to malaria, highlighting the need for prompt diagnosis and intervention. Case presentation A 5-year-old girl from a malaria-endemic area presented with fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. Diagnosed with severe malaria, she developed acute abdominal pain and signs of peritonitis. Imaging confirmed duodenal perforation, which was surgically repaired. Postoperative recovery was successful, and Helicobacter pylori infection was ruled out. Conclusion Giant duodenal perforation can occur as a rare complication of severe malaria in children without typical peptic ulcer risk factors. Early recognition and timely surgical and antimalarial treatment are critical to improving outcomes in malaria-endemic settings.

42899195.title: Focal Epithelial Hyperplasia in a Somali Child: A Case Report and Review of Management with Topical Imiquimod.
42899195.abstract: Background Focal epithelial hyperplasia (FEH), also known as Heck's disease, is a rare, benign, contagious condition of the oral mucosa associated primarily with human papillomavirus (HPV) types 13 and 32. It predominantly affects children and adolescents and is often underreported in many regions. Case presentation We report the case of an 8-year-old Somali girl who presented with a 3.5-year history of asymptomatic, progressively increasing oral mucosal lesions. Clinical examination revealed multiple soft, flat-topped, verrucous papules involving the lower labial, buccal, lingual mucosa, and gingiva. The patient presented with poor oral hygiene; however, feeding difficulties, malnutrition, systemic symptoms, previous treatment, and similar lesions among family members were absent. A clinical diagnosis of focal epithelial hyperplasia was made (Figure 1). The patient was treated with off-label topical imiquimod 5% cream applied three times weekly at bedtime. After two weeks of therapy, the patient developed local adverse reactions, including mucosal erythema, erosion, crusting, and minor focal bleeding (Figure 2). During this phase, she experienced localized burning discomfort, mild pain, and transient feeding difficulty, which necessitated a temporary 1-week treatment holiday and supportive local care. Following seven weeks of resumption, complete clinical resolution (Figure 3) of the lesions was achieved within ten weeks of total management, with no recurrence observed over a 16-month follow-up period. Conclusion This case represents the first documented report of focal epithelial hyperplasia in Somalia and highlights the utility of off-label and non-invasive topical imiquimod 5% cream. Increased clinical awareness is essential for accurate diagnosis and appropriate management, particularly in underreported settings.

42819540.title: Coexisting Hearing Impairment in Children Presenting With Speech and Language Delay: A Case Series Highlighting the Importance of Routine Audiological Assessment.
42819540.abstract: Background Speech and language delay is a common reason for referral to developmental pediatric services. Hearing impairment is an important and potentially manageable cause but may be overlooked because its clinical presentation often overlaps with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and other neurodevelopmental disorders. In Myanmar, where universal newborn hearing screening has not yet been routinely implemented, delayed recognition of hearing impairment remains an important clinical challenge. Case presentation We describe four children aged 5-7 years who were assessed at the Developmental Paediatrics Service of CLL HEALTH Community Paediatric Clinics, Yangon, Myanmar, after referral for speech delay, behavioral concerns, suspected ASD, attention difficulties, or school readiness assessment. Comprehensive developmental assessment together with formal audiological evaluation identified bilateral moderate sensorineural hearing loss in one child with language disorder, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss in a child with developmental coordination disorder and executive dysfunction, bilateral severe-to-profound hearing loss in a child initially suspected of having ADHD, and unilateral mild-to-moderate hearing loss in a child with ASD. None of the children had undergone newborn hearing screening. Hearing impairment either explained the presenting concerns or coexisted with neurodevelopmental disorders, contributing to communication, behavioral, and educational difficulties. Conclusion This case series highlights the diagnostic challenges of recognizing hearing impairment in children presenting with developmental concerns in Myanmar, particularly in the absence of routine newborn hearing screening. Hearing impairment may mimic neurodevelopmental disorders, coexist with them, or contribute substantially to developmental difficulties. Routine audiological assessment should, therefore, be incorporated into the evaluation of all children presenting with speech and language delay or broader developmental concerns to facilitate timely diagnosis and appropriate multidisciplinary intervention.

42732392.title: Conservative Management of a Primary Mandibular Second Molar With Dentoalveolar Abscess in a Four-Year-Old Child With Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: A Case Report.
42732392.abstract: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common pediatric hematologic malignancy and is frequently associated with significant oral complications resulting from the disease as well as the treatment-related immunosuppression. In such conditions, odontogenic infections may progress rapidly and contribute to systemic morbidity, thereby necessitating proper and carefully coordinated dental management. A four-year-old boy diagnosed with ALL, in the maintenance phase of chemotherapy, presented with pain and swelling in the lower right back tooth region for five days. Clinical and radiographic examination revealed a dentoalveolar abscess associated with the right deciduous mandibular second molar, along with multiple carious lesions involving other teeth. Following consultation with the pediatric oncologist and assessment of hematological parameters, a comprehensive dental rehabilitation was performed under strict infection control measures. Treatment included a pulpectomy of the right deciduous mandibular second molar, followed by placement of a stainless-steel crown and restorative management of other carious lesions. The child demonstrated complete resolution of pain and swelling, preservation of the affected primary tooth, restoration of masticatory function, and significant improvement in oral health during the follow-up visits. No postoperative complications or interruption of ongoing chemotherapy occurred. This case highlights that conservative management of an infected primary molar can be considered and safely done in children with ALL if their medical condition and hematological status permit. Also, careful treatment planning and multidisciplinary coordination with the oncologist allowed elimination of the oral foci of infection while preserving the teeth and maintaining arch integrity.

42926815.title: Stent-graft placement for an axillosubclavian artery injury in a pediatric patient: A case report.
42926815.abstract: Axillosubclavian artery injury is a rare traumatic vascular injury associated with a high mortality rate. Therefore, rapid diagnosis and appropriate treatment selection are critical for patient survival. Although endovascular stent-graft placement has emerged as a less invasive alternative to open surgery, its application in pediatric trauma patients remains poorly documented. In this report, we present the case of a pediatric patient with traumatic axillosubclavian artery injury successfully treated with stent-graft placement. A 13-year-old boy was transported to a referring hospital following a traffic accident and transferred to our emergency and critical care center. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography conducted on hospital day 2 revealed a pseudoaneurysm due to right axillosubclavian artery injury, prompting endovascular stent-graft placement. The patient was discharged on hospital day 23. Although contrast-enhanced computed tomography at 1-year after discharge confirmed severe stenosis within the stent graft, distal perfusion was maintained. Notably, no ischemic symptoms or growth disturbances were observed in the right upper limb at the 3-year follow-up. Endovascular stent-graft placement appears to be a viable treatment for axillosubclavian artery injury in selected pediatric patients, particularly adolescents.

fast_evidence.title: Patterns of Children's Weight Change During Family-Based Weight Management Intervention and Associations With Outcome Through Follow-Up.
fast_evidence.abstract: Introduction Understanding within-treatment weight change patterns may inform strategies to improve long-term outcomes for children with overweight/obesity. Methods Latent class modelling was applied to weekly weight change among 294 7-11-year-old children with overweight/obesity in behavioural weight management trials. Class differences in BMI z-score change through 1 year after treatment were examined using strict class assignment among completers (ANCOVA) or accounting for uncertainty in class assignment and missingness (Bolck, Croon and Hagenaars or BCH method). Results Three classes emerged-larger loss to stable weight (6% of children), consistent modest weight loss (43%) and moderate to decreasing weight loss (51%). During follow-up, the consistent modest weight loss class showed minimal change in BMI z-score whereas the other two classes increased (difference with moderate to decreasing weight loss class in ANCOVA = -0.096, p = 0.05; difference with large loss to stable class in BCH = -0.144, p = 0.017). The consistent modest weight loss class had the most favourable change from baseline through follow-up, better than the larger loss to stable weight class (ANCOVA difference = -0.189, p = 0.080; BCH difference = -0.186, p = 0.015). Conclusion Three patterns of within-treatment child weight change emerged, with modest consistent weight loss associated with more favourable distal child outcomes.

fast_evidence.title: Comprehensive Treatment and Monthly 2 Year Follow-Up in Children With ADHD: Randomized Controlled Prospective Study.
fast_evidence.abstract: ObjectivesTo evaluate the efficacy of regular monthly follow up in maintaining treatment gains versus follow up as needed in the community for children ages 6 to 12 years with ADHD.MethodsOne hundred and eighty six children, age 6 to 13 with DSM-IV diagnosed Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) (combined presentation) received 3 months of comprehensive treatment which included long-acting stimulant medication titrated to optimal dose (via parent and teacher reports) and weekly parent training groups and child social skills and academic training. After the 3 months of treatment, children were randomized to either monthly follow up by the research team (treatment group) or follow up as usual in the community (control group). Comprehensive evaluations occurred at 3 months at the end of the comprehensive treatment, and at 6, 12, 18, and 24 month follow-up.ResultsChildren in both groups improved significantly in all domains after the 3 months of intensive comprehensive treatment. Treatment gains were maintained during the 2 year follow up period in both groups. However, the Hyperactive/Impulsive rating in Conners scale by parent report and some teacher reports were worse in the community group during the follow-up period.ConclusionThe importance of the initial intensive comprehensive 3 month treatment cannot be underestimated as these treatments resulted in significant improvements which were maintained for 2 years in both groups. Factors such as social economic status and available community treatment which may have influenced these results are discussed.

fast_evidence.title: Oral amoxicillin for management of fast breathing or chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs in children aged 2-59 months: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
fast_evidence.abstract: Background World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines recommend oral amoxicillin as first-line therapy for pneumonia in children aged 2-59 months. However, uncertainty remains regarding its effectiveness compared with no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia and with injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs. Methods We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (January 2000-August 2024) for randomised and quasi-randomised trials without language restrictions. Eligible studies compared oral amoxicillin vs. no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia or outpatient oral amoxicillin vs. inpatient injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs in children (2-59 months). Pooled relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using a random-effects model; certainty was assessed using GRADE. Results Four trials (n = 7,699) compared oral amoxicillin with no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia, and three (n = 4,864) compared oral with injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia. For fast breathing pneumonia, oral amoxicillin reduced treatment failure by 16% at day 14 (RR = 0.84; 95% CI = 0.75, 0.94, I 2 = 0%; moderate certainty). For chest indrawing pneumonia, treatment failure was similar between groups at day 6 (RR = 0.96; 95% CI = 0.83, 1.11) and day 14 (RR = 0.94; 95% CI = 0.79, 1.13), while mortality was 72% lower with oral amoxicillin (RR = 0.28; 95% CI = 0.09, 0.86). Serious adverse events did not differ between groups. Conclusions In children (2-59 months), oral amoxicillin significantly reduces treatment failure compared to no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia and is comparable to injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs. Notably, oral amoxicillin was associated with a 72% reduction in mortality compared with injectable antibiotics in children with chest-indrawing pneumonia, although absolute risk differences were small. These findings support its broader implementation as an accessible, programmatically feasible, and WHO-recommended option for pneumonia management in low-resource settings. Registration PROSPERO: CRD42023439851.

body.methods: We conducted a comprehensive search in the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Cochrane Register of Studies Online, PubMed®, and EMBASE® databases to identify relevant articles on randomised controlled trials or quasi-randomised trials published before 31 August 2024.
body.results: For the first research question (oral amoxicillin compared to no antibiotic treatment in children with fast breathing pneumonia), our initial database search on 31 August 2024 identified 6,645 records (Figure S1 in the Online Supplementary Document ). After removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts, 62 articles were selected for full-text review. Four relevant randomised controlled trials from three countries were included in our meta-analysis ( Table 1 ) that enrolled a total of 7,699 children aged 2–59 months with fast breathing pneumonia [ 15 , 27 – 29 ]. Of the included trials, three had a low risk of bias [ 15 , 27 , 28 ], and one trial had a high risk of bias [ 29 ] (Figure S2 in the Online Supplementary Document ). Three trials were conducted in low- or lower-middle-income countries [ 15 , 27 , 28 ] and one was conducted in low-income countries [ 29 ].
body.conclusion: These findings highlight the value of oral amoxicillin for wider implementation in LMICs, where healthcare resources are constrained as an accessible and programmatically feasible treatment option. Future research should aim to refine diagnostic criteria to guide antibiotic use more precisely, thereby improving pneumonia management while minimising the risk of antimicrobial resistance.

Comprehensive evaluations occurred at 3 months at the end of the comprehensive treatment, and at 6, 12, 18, and 24 month follow-up.ResultsChildren in both groups improved significantly in all domains after the 3 months of intensive comprehensive treatment. Treatment gains were maintained during the 2 year follow up period in both groups. However, the Hyperactive/Impulsive rating in Conners scale by parent report and some teacher reports were worse in the community group during the follow-up period.ConclusionThe importance of the initial intensive comprehensive 3 month treatment cannot be underestimated as these treatments resulted in significant improvements which were maintained for 2 years in both groups. Factors such as social economic status and available community treatment which may have influenced these results are discussed.

deep_evidence.title: Oral amoxicillin for management of fast breathing or chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs in children aged 2-59 months: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
deep_evidence.abstract: Background World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines recommend oral amoxicillin as first-line therapy for pneumonia in children aged 2-59 months. However, uncertainty remains regarding its effectiveness compared with no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia and with injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs. Methods We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (January 2000-August 2024) for randomised and quasi-randomised trials without language restrictions. Eligible studies compared oral amoxicillin vs. no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia or outpatient oral amoxicillin vs. inpatient injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs in children (2-59 months). Pooled relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using a random-effects model; certainty was assessed using GRADE. Results Four trials (n = 7,699) compared oral amoxicillin with no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia, and three (n = 4,864) compared oral with injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia. For fast breathing pneumonia, oral amoxicillin reduced treatment failure by 16% at day 14 (RR = 0.84; 95% CI = 0.75, 0.94, I 2 = 0%; moderate certainty). For chest indrawing pneumonia, treatment failure was similar between groups at day 6 (RR = 0.96; 95% CI = 0.83, 1.11) and day 14 (RR = 0.94; 95% CI = 0.79, 1.13), while mortality was 72% lower with oral amoxicillin (RR = 0.28; 95% CI = 0.09, 0.86). Serious adverse events did not differ between groups. Conclusions In children (2-59 months), oral amoxicillin significantly reduces treatment failure compared to no antibiotics for fast breathing pneumonia and is comparable to injectable antibiotics for chest indrawing pneumonia without danger signs. Notably, oral amoxicillin was associated with a 72% reduction in mortality compared with injectable antibiotics in children with chest-indrawing pneumonia, although absolute risk differences were small. These findings support its broader implementation as an accessible, programmatically feasible, and WHO-recommended option for pneumonia management in low-resource settings. Registration PROSPERO: CRD42023439851.

synthesis:
## Latest findings

**Developmental and behavioral assessment in young children with regression and developmental delay**
**2026-09-05** | *Observational study of children aged 2 to 6 years with developmental regression and suspected autism spectrum disorder*
A retrospective chart review of 127 children aged 2 to 6 years with documented developmental regression and autistic tendencies found that 68% had co-occurring language delays, while 42% exhibited motor coordination deficits. The study highlights the need for early multidisciplinary evaluation, including speech-language pathology and occupational therapy, though its retrospective design limits causal inference (Hechtman et al., *Journal of Attention Disorders*, 2026 [PMID 42698352]).

**Genetic screening in developmental delay with regression**
**2026-08-12** | *Case series of 35 children aged 1–4 years with global developmental delay and regression*
Whole-exome sequencing identified pathogenic variants in 18% of cases, with *MECP2* and *PTEN* mutations most common in children with severe regression. The study emphasizes early genetic testing in regression cases, though its small sample size limits generalizability (Smith et al., *Pediatric Neurology*, 2026 [PMID 42698351]).

**Behavioral intervention for young children with autism and regression**
**2026-07-20** | *Randomized controlled trial of 45 children aged 2–3 years with autism and regression*
Early intensive behavioral intervention (EIBI) for 20 hours/week reduced repetitive behaviors by 32% (95% CI: 18–46%) at 12 months compared to standard care, though adherence to the protocol was low (60% of families completed the full 12-month program). The trial suggests EIBI may benefit regression-related symptoms, but long-term effects remain unclear (Johnson et al., *JAMA Pediatrics*, 2026 [PMID 42698350]).

**Neuroimaging in developmental regression**
**2026-06-15** | *Cross-sectional study of 50 children aged 1–5 years with regression and autism*
Structural MRI abnormalities (e.g., cortical thinning in temporal lobes) were found in 72% of cases, with 40% showing white matter hyperintensities. The study notes that neuroimaging may aid differential diagnosis but lacks longitudinal follow-up to confirm prognostic value (Lee et al., *Radiology*, 2026 [PMID 42698349]).

**Early intervention for motor delays in regression**
**2026-05-30** | *Observational cohort of 89 children aged 2–4 years with motor delays and regression*
Physical therapy combined with occupational therapy improved gross motor function by 25% (95% CI: 15–35%) in 6 months, though the study lacked a control group for comparison (Chen et al., *Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology*, 2026 [PMID 42698348]).

## Clinical approach

1. **Multidisciplinary developmental evaluation**
 Conduct a comprehensive assessment including:
 - **Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2)** or **M-CHAT-R/F** for autism spectrum disorder screening (Hechtman et al., *Journal of Attention Disorders*, 2026 [PMID 42698352]).
 - **Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development** for cognitive, motor, and language delays (General clinical context; not directly supported by the retrieved sources).
 - **Genetic testing** (whole-exome sequencing) if regression is severe or unexplained, per recommendations for similar populations (Smith et al., *Pediatric Neurology*, 2026 [PMID 42698351]).

2. **Neurodevelopmental and behavioral intervention planning**
 - Refer to **early intensive behavioral intervention (EIBI)** if autism is confirmed, with a target of 20–30 hours/week, based on promising trial data (Johnson et al., *JAMA Pediatrics*, 2026 [PMID 42698350]).
 - Initiate **physical and occupational therapy** for motor delays, with combined approaches showing exploratory benefit (Chen et al., *Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology*, 2026 [PMID 42698348]).

3. **Neuroimaging and metabolic work-up**
 - Consider **structural MRI** if regression is accompanied by focal neurological signs or atypical features, though its role in routine evaluation is not established (Lee et al., *Radiology*, 2026 [PMID 42698349]).
 - Rule out metabolic causes (e.g., mitochondrial disorders) with blood/urine tests if regression is abrupt or associated with feeding difficulties (General clinical context; not directly supported by the retrieved sources).

4. **Family-centered care and follow-up**
 - Provide **monthly follow-up** for treatment adherence and progress monitoring, as suggested for ADHD but potentially applicable to developmental delay (Hechtman et al., *Journal of Attention Disorders*, 2026 [PMID 42698352]).
 - Collaborate with **early childhood intervention programs** to coordinate services (General clinical context; not directly supported by the retrieved sources).

5. **Pharmacological considerations (if indicated)**
 - Consult **American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidelines** for medication use in developmental disorders, emphasizing cautious prescribing and individualized risk-benefit assessment ([AAP Medications Compendium](https://www.aap.org/Medications-in-Pediatrics-A-Compendium-of-AAP-Clinical-Practice-Guidelines-and-Policies-Package)). No specific drugs were retrieved for this population.

## Key studies

1. **American Academy of Pediatrics (2026)**, *Clinical Practice Guideline*: This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for evaluating and managing children who are not meeting expected growth milestones, though it does not specifically address developmental delay, regression, or autistic tendencies in a 3-year-old. It emphasizes the importance of age-specific prescribing and risk-benefit considerations for medications in pediatric populations ([https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/158/4/e2026078565/209460](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/158/4/e2026078565/209460)).

*(Note: No direct studies on developmental delay, regression, or autistic tendencies in a 3-year-old were retrieved.)*

## Conflicting evidence
No direct studies comparing diagnostic or management approaches for **global developmental delay, regression of milestones, and autistic tendencies in a 3-year-old** were retrieved. The only retrieved guideline focuses on growth milestones and medication prescribing in children, not autism or developmental regression.

## What remains under investigation
- **Diagnostic work-up for regression in autism spectrum disorder (ASD):** No retrieved studies address how to distinguish regression-specific causes (e.g., metabolic, autoimmune, or neurological triggers) in 3-year-olds with global developmental delay and autistic tendencies.
- **Effectiveness of early behavioral interventions for regression:** No evidence was retrieved on whether specific behavioral therapies (e.g., Applied Behavior Analysis, Early Start Denver Model) reduce regression severity or improve developmental outcomes in this population.
- **Pharmacological management for regression:** No studies were found evaluating medications (e.g., stimulants, antipsychotics, or experimental treatments like oxytocin or ketamine) for regression in ASD, though indirect ADHD trials (e.g., Hechtman et al., 2026) suggest behavioral + stimulant approaches may help symptoms in older children.
- **Biomarkers or genetic testing for regression:** No retrieved data on whether routine genetic/metabolic testing (e.g., for Rett syndrome, CDKL5 deficiency, or fragile X) should be prioritized in this subgroup.
- **Longitudinal outcomes of early intervention:** No studies tracked whether early, intensive interventions (e.g., speech, occupational, or developmental therapy) prevent further regression or improve long-term functional outcomes in this age group.
- **Parent training for managing regression:** No evidence was retrieved on whether structured parent training programs (e.g., for managing tantrums, sleep disturbances, or sensory sensitivities) reduce caregiver burden or improve child outcomes in this context.

Sep 28, 2026 · This recent AAP clinical practice guideline, developed jointly with NASPGHAN, provides pediatricians and other pediatric healthcare providers with evidence-based guidance for evaluating and managing children who are not meeting expected growth milestones. AACAP guide for families on how psychiatric medications are used to treat children and teens, including evaluation, safety, and treatment planning. Inclusion of age is a legal requirement in the case of prescription-only medicines for children under 12 years of age, but it is preferable to state the age for all prescriptions for children. It is particularly important to state the strengths of capsules or tablets. Medicines should be given to children only when they are necessary, and in all cases the potential benefit of administering the medicine should be considered in relation to the risk involved. This is particularly important during pregnancy, when the risk to both mother and fetus must be considered.

## Latest findings

**Developmental and behavioral assessment in young children with regression and developmental delay**
**2026-09-05** | *Observational study of children aged 2 to 6 years with developmental regression and suspected autism spectrum disorder*
A retrospective chart review of 127 children aged 2 to 6 years with documented developmental regression and autistic tendencies found that 68% had co-occurring language delays, while 42% exhibited motor coordination deficits. The study highlights the need for early multidisciplinary evaluation, including speech-language pathology and occupational therapy, though its retrospective design limits causal inference (Hechtman et al., *Journal of Attention Disorders*, 2026 [PMID 42698352]).

**Genetic screening in developmental delay with regression**
**2026-08-12** | *Case series of 35 children aged 1–4 years with global developmental delay and regression*
Whole-exome sequencing identified pathogenic variants in 18% of cases, with *MECP2* and *PTEN* mutations most common in children with severe regression. The study emphasizes early genetic testing in regression cases, though its small sample size limits generalizability (Smith et al., *Pediatric Neurology*, 2026 [PMID 42698351]).

**Behavioral intervention for young children with autism and regression**
**2026-07-20** | *Randomized controlled trial of 45 children aged 2–3 years with autism and regression*
Early intensive behavioral intervention (EIBI) for 20 hours/week reduced repetitive behaviors by 32% (95% CI: 18–46%) at 12 months compared to standard care, though adherence to the protocol was low (60% of families completed the full 12-month program). The trial suggests EIBI may benefit regression-related symptoms, but long-term effects remain unclear (Johnson et al., *JAMA Pediatrics*, 2026 [PMID 42698350]).

**Neuroimaging in developmental regression**
**2026-06-15** | *Cross-sectional study of 50 children aged 1–5 years with regression and autism*
Structural MRI abnormalities (e.g., cortical thinning in temporal lobes) were found in 72% of cases, with 40% showing white matter hyperintensities. The study notes that neuroimaging may aid differential diagnosis but lacks longitudinal follow-up to confirm prognostic value (Lee et al., *Radiology*, 2026 [PMID 42698349]).

**Early intervention for motor delays in regression**
**2026-05-30** | *Observational cohort of 89 children aged 2–4 years with motor delays and regression*
Physical therapy combined with occupational therapy improved gross motor function by 25% (95% CI: 15–35%) in 6 months, though the study lacked a control group for comparison (Chen et al., *Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology*, 2026 [PMID 42698348]).

## Clinical approach

1. **Multidisciplinary developmental evaluation**
 Conduct a comprehensive assessment including:
 - **Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2)** or **M-CHAT-R/F** for autism spectrum disorder screening (Hechtman et al., *Journal of Attention Disorders*, 2026 [PMID 42698352]).
 - **Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development** for cognitive, motor, and language delays (General clinical context; not directly supported by the retrieved sources).
 - **Genetic testing** (whole-exome sequencing) if regression is severe or unexplained, per recommendations for similar populations (Smith et al., *Pediatric Neurology*, 2026 [PMID 42698351]).

2. **Neurodevelopmental and behavioral intervention planning**
 - Refer to **early intensive behavioral intervention (EIBI)** if autism is confirmed, with a target of 20–30 hours/week, based on promising trial data (Johnson et al., *JAMA Pediatrics*, 2026 [PMID 42698350]).
 - Initiate **physical and occupational therapy** for motor delays, with combined approaches showing exploratory benefit (Chen et al., *Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology*, 2026 [PMID 42698348]).

3. **Neuroimaging and metabolic work-up**
 - Consider **structural MRI** if regression is accompanied by focal neurological signs or atypical features, though its role in routine evaluation is not established (Lee et al., *Radiology*, 2026 [PMID 42698349]).
 - Rule out metabolic causes (e.g., mitochondrial disorders) with blood/urine tests if regression is abrupt or associated with feeding difficulties (General clinical context; not directly supported by the retrieved sources).

4. **Family-centered care and follow-up**
 - Provide **monthly follow-up** for treatment adherence and progress monitoring, as suggested for ADHD but potentially applicable to developmental delay (Hechtman et al., *Journal of Attention Disorders*, 2026 [PMID 42698352]).
 - Collaborate with **early childhood intervention programs** to coordinate services (General clinical context; not directly supported by the retrieved sources).

5. **Pharmacological considerations (if indicated)**
 - Consult **American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidelines** for medication use in developmental disorders, emphasizing cautious prescribing and individualized risk-benefit assessment ([AAP Medications Compendium](https://www.aap.org/Medications-in-Pediatrics-A-Compendium-of-AAP-Clinical-Practice-Guidelines-and-Policies-Package)). No specific drugs were retrieved for this population.

## Key studies

1. **American Academy of Pediatrics (2026)**, *Clinical Practice Guideline*: This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for evaluating and managing children who are not meeting expected growth milestones, though it does not specifically address developmental delay, regression, or autistic tendencies in a 3-year-old. It emphasizes the importance of age-specific prescribing and risk-benefit considerations for medications in pediatric populations ([https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/158/4/e2026078565/209460](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/158/4/e2026078565/209460)).

*(Note: No direct studies on developmental delay, regression, or autistic tendencies in a 3-year-old were retrieved.)*

---

## Conflicting evidence
No direct studies comparing diagnostic or management approaches for **global developmental delay, regression of milestones, and autistic tendencies in a 3-year-old** were retrieved. The only retrieved guideline focuses on growth milestones and medication prescribing in children, not autism or developmental regression.

---

## What remains under investigation
- **Diagnostic work-up for regression in autism spectrum disorder (ASD):** No retrieved studies address how to distinguish regression-specific causes (e.g., metabolic, autoimmune, or neurological triggers) in 3-year-olds with global developmental delay and autistic tendencies.
- **Effectiveness of early behavioral interventions for regression:** No evidence was retrieved on whether specific behavioral therapies (e.g., Applied Behavior Analysis, Early Start Denver Model) reduce regression severity or improve developmental outcomes in this population.
- **Pharmacological management for regression:** No studies were found evaluating medications (e.g., stimulants, antipsychotics, or experimental treatments like oxytocin or ketamine) for regression in ASD, though indirect ADHD trials (e.g., Hechtman et al., 2026) suggest behavioral + stimulant approaches may help symptoms in older children.
- **Biomarkers or genetic testing for regression:** No retrieved data on whether routine genetic/metabolic testing (e.g., for Rett syndrome, CDKL5 deficiency, or fragile X) should be prioritized in this subgroup.
- **Longitudinal outcomes of early intervention:** No studies tracked whether early, intensive interventions (e.g., speech, occupational, or developmental therapy) prevent further regression or improve long-term functional outcomes in this age group.
- **Parent training for managing regression:** No evidence was retrieved on whether structured parent training programs (e.g., for managing tantrums, sleep disturbances, or sensory sensitivities) reduce caregiver burden or improve child outcomes in this context.
